summary: Defines the ORIGIN frame for HTTP/3. The frame already exists for HTTP/2 and applies equally well to HTTP/3, but it needs to be separately registered.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9412 defines the ORIGIN frame for HTTP/3. A server sends it on its control stream to tell the client which origins the connection can serve.

subtitle: The HTTP/2 ORIGIN frame adapted for use on an HTTP/3 control stream.

tldr.problem: The ORIGIN frame already defined for HTTP/2 is useful in HTTP/3 but requires a separate HTTP/3 frame registration and stream mapping.
tldr.mechanism: An HTTP/3 server sends an ORIGIN frame on its control stream with length-delimited ASCII origin entries.
tldr.outcome: The frame tells the client which origins the server asserts the connection is or could be authoritative for.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 9412's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC registers the ORIGIN frame for HTTP/3.

sections.title: Bringing ORIGIN to HTTP/3
sections.content:
The HTTP/2 ORIGIN frame indicates which origins are available on a connection. The frame's semantics also apply to HTTP/3, but HTTP/3 needs its own registered frame type.

HTTP/2 uses stream 0 for connection-level frames. HTTP/3 instead uses a pair of unidirectional control streams, so the ORIGIN frame is sent from the server to the client on the server's control stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The frame carries the same kind of origin information in HTTP/3 as in HTTP/2. HTTP/3 sends it on a control stream instead of stream 0.

sections.title: The ORIGIN Frame Layout
sections.content:
The ORIGIN frame type is 0x0c, or decimal 12. Its payload contains zero or more Origin-Entry fields, each with a 16-bit length followed by an ASCII serialization of an origin.

The origin entry is length-delimited. The sender asserts that the connection is or could be authoritative for the listed origin.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry gives the length of an origin string and then the string itself. The server uses the frame to list origins associated with the connection.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no security considerations beyond those discussed for the HTTP/2 ORIGIN frame and HTTP/3. It does not add a separate authentication or authorization mechanism for the origin entries.

The ORIGIN frame is a server assertion about origins associated with a connection, using the semantics of the referenced HTTP/2 frame specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The frame reuses the security considerations of HTTP/2 ORIGIN and HTTP/3. It does not define a new security mechanism for the list.
